description: Frequency measures how often something repeats per second, from once-per-cosmic-era cycles to electromagnetic radiation oscillating millions of trillions of times each second. Some entries here are direct oscillation frequencies, while others are derived from a reported period using frequency = 1 / period. That makes this dimension especially useful for connecting rotations, rhythms, waves, resonance, and light on a single logarithmic axis.
name: Frequency

description: This first-pass entropy scale focuses on entropy change, not total entropy and not raw microstate counts. That makes the dimension much more concrete: each item is a process like erasing a bit, melting ice, or vaporizing water. Temperature and process definitions matter a lot here, so qualifiers are especially important.
name: Entropy

description: Electric charge measures how much net positive or negative charge a system carries. This version now leans toward perspective-giving examples like static shocks, lightning, thunderclouds, batteries, and the Faraday constant rather than long ladders of arbitrary capacitors. The goal is to connect microscopic charge, biology, atmospheric electricity, and stored electrical systems on one axis.
name: Charge

description: Magnetic-field strength is expressed here as magnetic flux density in tesla. Some entries are ambient fields, some are surface fields of magnets or stars, and others are instrument fields from MRI scanners or laboratory magnets. The result is a scale that connects biology, everyday magnets, planets, plasma devices, and compact stars.
name: Magnetic Field

description: This scale stores acoustic intensity in watts per square meter, but by default it can be read in decibels because that is how people usually reason about loudness. Most source-side figures are reported in dB SPL and then converted into physical intensity for canonical storage, so the item names emphasize context such as distance from the source. That keeps whispers, appliances, traffic, thunder, jets, and launch pads on one comparable axis while still allowing direct intensity units when needed.
name: Loudness

description: This scale stores physical intensity as power per unit area in watts per square meter. It is meant for radiation, beams, and flux-like limits rather than photometric brightness or sound loudness. That makes it the natural home for solar irradiance, laser focus, collapse-threshold estimates, and the Planck-intensity scale.
name: Intensity

description: Length measures the distance between two points, yet it spans everything from the Planck length, where spacetime ripples like quantum foam, to the 93-billion-light-year reach of the observable universe. Across these 61 orders of magnitude, the same physical laws shape quarks, atoms, planets, and galaxies. If the universe were the size of Earth, a human would be smaller than an atom.
name: Length

description: Duration measures time intervals across everything from quantum events to cosmic evolution. Time gives us the framework for understanding cause and effect, change, and how things move toward disorder. This dimension covers both quick events and slow processes, showing us how time works from tiny particles to giant galaxies.
name: Duration

description: Mass tracks inertia and the amount of matter under a stated definition, from subatomic particles to galaxies. Some entries are direct measurements, while others are derived estimates such as the mass of a lake from its volume and density. Every item names the object and the measurement basis so the scale remains comparable.
name: Mass

description: Electric current measures how quickly charge moves through a circuit, membrane, plasma, or conductor. The examples now deliberately include biology, implants, consumer electronics, household power, heavy industry, and lightning so the scale is easier to orient yourself on. Some values are direct ratings, while others are stated as representative operating currents for a concrete scenario.
name: Current

description: Temperature measures how hot or cold a system is, but on a deeper level it tracks the distribution of energy among microscopic degrees of freedom. This makes it one of the rare scales that links kitchen experience, planetary climate, stellar interiors, and particle collisions. Many values are quoted directly in kelvin, while others are converted from Celsius or Fahrenheit values reported in the source.
name: Temperature

description: Counts are dimensionless tallies of discrete things or discrete possibilities: planets, genes, cells, books, stars, IPv6 addresses, or legal game states. Mixing literal inventories with combinatorial possibility spaces would be misleading if that distinction were hidden, so each entry says what is being counted. This scale is useful for comparing everyday finite sets with astronomical and computationally explosive counts on one logarithmic axis.
name: Counts

description: Brightness here refers to luminance, the light leaving or reflected by a surface per unit area in a given direction. It connects what your eye perceives on a screen or page to the photometric power behind it. Unlike illuminance on a desk, luminance belongs to the surface itself under stated conditions. Each item below specifies the scene and viewing context so the number has a clear meaning.
name: Brightness

description: Area here means a characteristic area under explicit qualifiers, often a surface area, cross-section, footprint, or geographic extent. Mixing those notions blindly would be misleading, so each entry states what kind of area is being used. The point is coverage across scales, not a claim that all areas answer the same question.
name: Area

description: Volume tracks three-dimensional extent under explicit geometric assumptions. Many values here are derived from a stated radius, diameter, or envelope shape rather than directly measured container capacity. Each item therefore includes a short qualifier describing whether it is a literal volume, an effective occupied volume, or an approximate geometric envelope.
name: Volume

description: Population density here means people per unit total land area. It is a clean way to compare remote regions, countries, city-states, boroughs, and extreme urban enclaves. Because jurisdiction boundaries matter, the label should always say what region is being measured.
name: Population Density

description: Physiological density is population divided by arable land area rather than total land area. That makes it a rough measure of how heavily a society leans on its food-producing land. It is more conceptually loaded than ordinary population density, so the arable-land qualifier is essential.
name: Physiological Density

description: Agricultural density is agricultural population divided by arable land area. It is often used to contrast labor-intensive farming with heavily mechanized farming. The numerator is not total population, so that qualifier should stay visible anywhere the value is shown.
name: Agricultural Density

description: Quality-adjusted life years compress length of life and quality of life into one metric. This is a powerful but highly model-dependent quantity, so each item should state whether it is a stock of healthy time, a gain from an intervention, or a loss from disability. It is useful here because it gives a common pedagogical axis for many health choices.
name: QALYs

description: A micromort is a one-in-a-million chance of death. It is especially useful for one-off acute risks like a skydive, a marathon, or a surgical procedure. Long-term chronic risks can be represented here too, but only if the time basis is stated explicitly.
name: Micromorts

description: This scale stores disease rarity as prevalence fraction, so higher values mean more common conditions and lower values mean rarer ones. It is intentionally simple and does not collapse incidence, prevalence, lifetime risk, and carrier frequency into one number unless that qualifier is stated. The frontend can later re-express these as “1 in N” when helpful.
name: Disease Rarity

description: This scale counts biological cells, from a single bacterium up to all bacteria on Earth. It is dimensionless mathematically but still extremely informative conceptually. Qualifiers matter because “cell count” can mean one organism, one tissue sample, or a planetary total.
name: Cell Count

description: Absorbed dose measures how much ionizing-radiation energy is deposited per kilogram. It spans dental X-rays, CT scans, cancer therapy, acute radiation syndrome, and industrial sterilization. Body part, fractionation, and exposure type matter enough here that the qualifiers should stay visible.
name: Absorbed Dose

description: Information here means a storage or message size expressed as bytes, whether the source talks about a literal file capacity, a memory size, or a derived information estimate. Some entries are direct capacities like discs and tapes, while others are derived from genome lengths, audio sample rates, or raw video formats. That makes this scale useful for comparing messages, media, genomes, and storage technologies on one logarithmic axis.
name: Information

description: Information rate measures how quickly symbols, bits, or higher-level messages move through a channel. Some entries here are literal interface or codec rates quoted directly by a standard, while others are derived from a source-side rate such as bytes per second or DNA bases per second. That lets one logarithmic axis connect teletypes, genomes, display links, Ethernet, and modern memory buses.
name: Information Rate

description: This scale treats FLOPs pragmatically as floating-point operations per second, the throughput measure most people mean when they compare processors, GPUs, AI accelerators, and supercomputers. It now includes AI-flavored reference points such as approximate LLM inference workloads and training-scale estimates alongside direct hardware specs. Precision mode still matters in real hardware, so the notes are representative rather than exhaustive.
name: FLOPs

description: Pressure is force per unit area, the intensity with which a surface is pressed. It explains why a stiletto heel dents wood while a snowshoe floats, even with the same weight. In fluids, pressure transmits uniformly and drives flow from high to low according to gradients. Every value below names a setting and condition so the number connects to daily life or specific experiments.
name: Pressure

description: Youngs modulus describes linear elastic stiffness, the ratio of stress to strain for small reversible deformations. It is the slope of the initial part of a stress strain curve under uniaxial load at stated temperature and rate. Microstructure, porosity, and moisture can shift it dramatically for natural materials. Each value below includes a representative condition so comparisons hold water.
name: Youngs Modulus

description: Yield strength marks the stress where a material stops returning to its original shape and begins to deform permanently. Engineers usually define it by a 0.2 percent offset on a tensile test curve at room temperature unless noted. The value depends strongly on processing, microstructure, and loading rate. Each entry states a representative condition so comparisons are meaningful.
name: Yield Strength

description: Density is mass per unit volume under stated composition, temperature, and pressure assumptions. Most entries below are bulk average densities rather than microscopic local densities, and extreme astrophysical entries are explicitly marked when they refer to stellar cores or degenerate matter.
name: Density

description: Dynamic viscosity measures how strongly a fluid resists being sheared or made to flow. Some entries are ordinary room-temperature liquids, others are effective viscosities for materials like glacier ice or the mantle that only flow over long timescales. Because viscosity changes strongly with temperature and composition, qualifiers matter here more than they do for many other scales.
name: Viscosity

description: Flow rate measures how much volume passes a boundary per unit time. This scale is useful for comparing microfluidics, medical drips, household plumbing, industrial systems, and the largest geophysical currents and rivers. Flow depends strongly on context, so representative operating conditions are part of the meaning.
name: Flow Rate

description: Surface tension is the energetic cost of creating more liquid surface, usually expressed as force per unit length. It is highly sensitive to temperature and contaminants, so these are representative values rather than immutable constants. This scale is useful for comparing cryogenic fluids, common liquids, and unusual high-tension metals.
name: Surface Tension

description: This salinity scale stores dissolved-salt content as mass fraction. That makes freshwater, blood plasma, seawater, brines, and hypersaline lakes comparable on one axis. The exact chemical makeup varies, so these are representative total-salinity benchmarks rather than precise ionic analyses.
name: Salinity

description: This phase-one concentration scale uses molar concentration, stored canonically in moles per cubic meter. It connects trace atmospheric or biochemical concentrations with laboratory solutions and nearly pure substances. Concentration is highly definition-sensitive, so each item states what is dissolved or counted.
name: Concentration

description: Hardness here is treated pragmatically as indentation hardness expressed in pascals where possible. This is not a perfect universal property because Mohs, Vickers, Brinell, and other hardness scales emphasize different tests. Still, a pressure-like canonical scale makes the ordering of soft metals, glass, carbides, and diamond easier to compare logarithmically.
name: Hardness

description: Strain is fractional deformation: how much a material stretches, compresses, or shears relative to its original size. It is dimensionless, but it is still highly informative across engineering, geology, and precision physics. This scale connects tiny metrological strains with yield strains and large deformations in soft materials.
name: Strain

description: Thermal conductivity measures how readily heat flows through a material under a temperature gradient. It helps connect insulators, building materials, fluids, metals, semiconductors, and diamond on one scale. Values depend on temperature, porosity, and orientation, so they should be read as representative rather than universal.
name: Thermal Conductivity

description: Specific heat capacity measures how much energy a kilogram of material needs to change temperature by one kelvin. This scale is good for intuition about why water moderates climate, why metals heat quickly, and why gases and cryogens behave so differently. Values depend on temperature and phase, so representative conditions matter.
name: Specific Heat

description: Energy measures the capacity to cause change, whether moving a mass, breaking a bond, or warming a room. In practice it ties together force, distance, and heat with a single bookkeeping number that must be conserved. For any process you care about, from a heartbeat to a supernova, energy is the currency that balances the before and after. Here we compare characteristic amounts for specific objects and conditions so the numbers map to lived experience.
name: Energy

description: Force quantifies how strongly an interaction changes motion or shape, linking directly to acceleration by Newton’s second law. In contact problems it is the agency behind pushes, pulls, and pressures; at a distance it expresses gravity and electromagnetism. Engineers budget forces to keep bridges stable and joints safe. Each entry below states the object and condition so the number is actionable, not abstract.
name: Force

description: Speed tells how fast position changes with time, without caring about the direction of travel. It is the scalar magnitude behind commuting, sprinting, and orbiting, the number you see on a speedometer. Human bodies sense acceleration more than speed, but fatigue and safety often map back to speed limits. Each entry below identifies a specific context so the values can be tested against experience or instruments.
name: Speed

description: **Acceleration** measures how quickly velocity changes, with direction indicating whether speed increases or decreases. It plays a key role in dynamics: objects feel forces through acceleration (e.g. the 1g free-fall of gravity) and extreme accelerations can stress materials or organisms. In our universe, accelerations range from the **gentlest** effects--like the tiny 10^(-10) m/s^2 acceleration of the expanding cosmos--to the **most violent** known, such as collisions of black holes or particle explosions. We explore this vast span from the nearly imperceptible to the practically inconceivable.
name: Acceleration

description: Jerk is the time rate of change of acceleration, indicating how abruptly a motion profile is being altered. Human comfort is strongly tied to jerk limits rather than raw acceleration because nerves respond to changes. Vehicles, elevators, and robots therefore shape motion with bounded jerk for smoothness. Each value below states the scenario and operating condition so the number maps to a real ride or mechanism.
name: Jerk

description: Torque measures rotational push: how strongly a force tries to twist something around an axis. This scale mixes microscopic rotary motors, hand tools, engines, and utility-scale machinery. Many values are representative operating torques rather than immutable constants, so the qualifiers and source notes matter.
name: Torque

description: Moment of inertia measures resistance to angular acceleration. It depends not just on mass but on how far that mass sits from the axis, which is why a bicycle wheel, a door, and the Earth can all appear here meaningfully. Values are always axis-specific, so the item label matters a lot.
name: Moment of Inertia

description: Angle measures rotational separation or apparent offset. This scale can represent anything from astronomical micro-offsets to human-scale fields of view and full turns. Because angles can be used both for geometry and for apparent size, the description of each item matters.
name: Angle

description: Angular velocity measures how fast something rotates. This scale connects orbital motion, clocks, household appliances, turbines, and compact stars. Many entries are converted from revolutions per minute or periods, so the derivations are intentionally exposed.
name: Angular Velocity

description: Scoville heat units are a familiar rough scale for pungency from capsaicinoids. They are not a fundamental physical unit, but they are pedagogically useful for comparing mild peppers, hot sauces, pepper sprays, and nearly pure capsaicin. Reported values often come as ranges, so the entries here use representative central values.
name: Scoville Heat

description: This first-pass odor scale is not “how smelly” in the abstract. It is the airborne concentration of a named odorant, usually in parts per billion by volume, which makes the axis more objective and shareable. Perception still depends on chemistry and thresholds, so the named compound is part of the data, not a side note.
name: Odor Concentration

description: This hearing-focused frequency scale emphasizes sound-producing or sound-perceiving systems rather than arbitrary oscillations. It connects musical pitch, voice, animal calls, ultrasound, and familiar engineering standards. Because many sources quote ranges, several items use representative center frequencies.
name: Sound Frequency

description: Visual angle measures how large something looks from a given viewpoint. It is one of the most direct ways to compare the apparent size of the Moon, a smartphone pixel, a doorway, or your whole field of view. These are geometry-driven values, so distance assumptions are part of the meaning.
name: Visual Angle

description: This roughness scale treats surface roughness as a characteristic amplitude, usually comparable to an Ra-style average roughness. It connects optical polishing, semiconductor surfaces, paper, skin, machined parts, and construction materials. Surface texture is method-dependent, so the labels and notes matter here more than for simpler geometric scales.
name: Roughness

description: The coefficient of friction is dimensionless, but it still forms a useful comparative scale across lubricated bearings, skis on snow, tires on asphalt, and gecko-inspired adhesion. The meaning depends on the material pair and on whether the value is static, kinetic, or rolling, so the item labels keep that context visible.
name: Coefficient of Friction

description: Cost translates human effort, resources, and time into a single comparable number denominated in money. It compresses supply chains, regulation, and risk into prices that move daily with geography and policy. For each entry, I specify a concrete item or service and the condition of purchase, such as retail, wholesale, or per unit time. The aim is scale and perspective rather than price quotes, so values are representative snapshots with context.
name: Costs

description: Historical time is stored here as years before the present, so that human memory, recorded history, deep prehistory, and cosmological time can live on one logarithmic axis. It overlaps with duration, but the emphasis is different: these entries are about how far back events sit from now, not how long a process lasted.
name: Historical Time

description: This scale measures how often discrete events happen, canonically in counts per second. It is intentionally broad: biological rhythms, industrial lines, social platforms, digital packets, and physical decays can all be compared once they are expressed as event rates. Each entry states what is being counted so unlike things are not silently conflated.
name: Counts per Unit Time

description: Probability measures how likely a specifically defined event is, from certainty down to essentially impossible random guesses. This is a natural logarithmic scale for rare events like jackpot wins, perfect brackets, and cryptographic hits. The event definition matters more here than almost anywhere else, so the labels are intentionally explicit.
name: Probability

description: This scale stores precision as relative uncertainty or fractional error. Smaller values mean higher precision, so it is inverted compared with everyday language like “more precise.” That inversion is worth it because relative uncertainty is much more coherent and log-friendly than a vague notion of accuracy.
name: Precision & Accuracy

description: This phase-one correlation scale stores the magnitude of Pearson correlation as |r|, from almost no linear association up to perfect correlation. The sign and domain context belong in qualifiers, because a strong negative correlation is just as strong as a strong positive one. This is useful pedagogically, but it is also easy to misuse: correlation depends on the variables chosen, sample definition, and whether the underlying relationship is actually linear.
name: Correlation Coefficient

description: This phase-one effect-size scale uses the magnitude of Cohen's d, the standardized difference between two means in units of standard deviations. It is more comparable than raw percentage changes, but only when the underlying comparison is well defined. Large values are genuinely dramatic because they imply groups separated by substantial fractions of a standard deviation or more.
name: Effect Size

description: This phase-one utility scale is intentionally a proxy: it stores welfare or utility in quality-adjusted life-year equivalents. That makes the values easier to compare with health and time scales, but it is not a universal theory of value. Use it as a pedagogical scaffold for “how much good or bad is this outcome roughly like,” not as a final moral ranking.
name: Utility

description: This scale treats attention pragmatically as person-seconds of engaged time. That is more comparable and more additive than raw views, impressions, or clicks, and it lets a glance, a lecture, a concert, and a livestream all live on one axis. Views and audience counts can still appear as qualifiers or source notes.
name: Attention
